name: David Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small firm that does loft conversions and extensions on older houses. There's Pete, who owns it, me, two other carpenters and whoever we bring in for plastering. My day's usually cutting new floor joists into a loft, building stud walls, fitting stairs, and talking the homeowner out of whatever they saw on a TV show. I love the puzzle of an old house, every one's been botched by someone different over 80 years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than people think. I scan the loft with my phone and an app turns it into a floor plan, then I get an AI assistant to help me work out the timber list and a rough price before Pete looks at it. I use it every day, for ordering, for checking building rules, even for writing nice emails to fussy clients. I live with my partner Lena, who's a primary school teacher, and we've got about three months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's still useful. At work I'd keep showing Pete the shortcuts. Online I'd probably say the hype was silly but the tools are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays the same, which is fine, and I keep my little edge because I'm quicker with the tools than most. My real plan is to have my own firm by 30 or so. That doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working for Pete, keep using AI for the pricing and ordering, and start doing a few small jobs on my own at weekends, like a stud wall or a staircase. Keep saving, maybe up to a hundred and eighty a month, so I've got a cushion when I go solo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go solo. What's the first step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting my own insurance and doing two or three weekend jobs that I price and run myself. Pete's fine with it as long as I don't poach his customers. He's 55 and talks about retiring, so it might work out for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the tools don't get any better than they are now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm still ahead, because most small builders barely use them. A good price in a day instead of a week wins jobs. That's enough of an edge for me.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's still useful, and keep showing Pete the shortcuts. Online I'd say the hype was silly but the tools are good.
S0.think: My job stays the same and I keep my edge from being quicker with the tools than most. My plan for my own firm by about 30 doesn't change.
S0.do: Keeps working for Pete and using AI for pricing and ordering, and starts doing small weekend jobs on his own. Raises savings to about a hundred and eighty a month as a cushion for going solo.
S0.quote: A good price in a day instead of a week wins jobs.
S0.fieldNote: David already uses AI daily and sees it as his edge over other small builders. His focus is his own business, and his boss's retirement is a quiet opportunity. He's practical rather than political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal, but builders who use it will do fine. I'd tell the lads at work to get on board. I wouldn't say it's good or bad, just that it's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is my chance. Pricing, planning and paperwork are a third of running a firm, and if AI does that, a small outfit like mine could compete with the big ones. Some of the older builders would struggle, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go solo sooner, maybe within a year, and set up everything to run with AI from day one. I'd spend a couple of thousand on a proper laser scanner and better software. If there were robot tools for lifting or cutting on site, I'd try them early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited, a little nervous about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two thousand is a big chunk of three months' savings. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Lena would ask the same. I'd probably wait until I had three solid jobs booked before buying it. I'm keen, not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle, in your world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete's friend Barry, who prices everything on the back of a cigarette packet and is always wrong. He's brilliant with his hands, but if clients expect a price in a day, he'll lose work. I'd maybe offer to do his pricing for a cut.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big deal, but builders who use it will do fine, and tell the lads at work to get on board. It's not good or bad, just happening.
S1.think: This is my chance, because if AI handles pricing, planning and paperwork, a small firm could compete with big ones. Some older builders would struggle.
S1.do: Goes solo within about a year with AI set up from day one, and spends a couple of thousand on a laser scanner and software once three jobs are booked. Tries robot lifting or cutting tools early.
S1.feel: Excited, a little nervous about the money.
S1.quote: I'd probably wait until I had three solid jobs booked before buying it. I'm keen, not daft.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady disruption as an opening for a small business. He's careful with money despite his appetite for new tools. He even sees a side line in doing pricing for older builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be rough for a lot of people and nobody's ready. I'd tell everyone to get some savings together. I wouldn't be shouting about who to blame, there'd be no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my business plan dies. If an AI with robots can do a loft conversion, why would anyone pay me? My edge was being better with the tools, and in two years everyone has the tools and the tools do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't go solo, I'd stay with Pete for the steady wage and save every bit I could. I'd try to be the person who sets up and checks the robot work on Pete's jobs, because someone has to sign off a structure. I'd learn everything about the robot kit as soon as it was out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I had things to try, but the ground would feel soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to sign off a structure. Are you sure of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure at all. It's what I'd hope. If the AI can do the engineering too, then it's down to the rules and whether people trust a robot in their loft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say at least teaching's safe, and then she'd stop and think about it. She uses AI for lesson plans already. We'd probably both be wondering, but her job's more about kids being with a person.

S2.say: I'd say this will be rough for many people and nobody's ready, and tell everyone to save. I wouldn't bother shouting about who to blame.
S2.think: My business plan dies, because if AI with robots can do a loft conversion, nobody pays me. My edge was being better with tools, and soon the tools do the work.
S2.do: Drops the plan to go solo, stays with Pete for the steady wage and saves everything he can. Tries to become the person who sets up and checks robot work on jobs, learning the kit as soon as it's out.
S2.feel: Anxious, with things still to try but the ground feeling soft.
S2.quote: My edge was being better with the tools, and in two years everyone has the tools and the tools do the work.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version turns his biggest strength into nothing, and he sees that clearly. He doesn't freeze; he switches from building a business to protecting income and staying close to the new kit. He's honest that his hope of signing off robot work may not hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable if you move now. I'd tell the lads to learn the robot stuff while it's coming in. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the window for my own firm is about three years. Long enough to make some money and buy kit, not long enough to retire on. After that, the firm might be a few robots and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Pete about buying into his firm instead of starting my own, so I get his customers and his name. I'd use my savings and maybe a small loan, and put the money into robot tools as soon as they're good. I'd learn how to run and price robot jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but up for it. Like starting a big job with a tight deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan with five years to go. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd keep it small and short, paid off in three years. If I can't make that work, I won't do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the firm look like in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, maybe one other person, a couple of robots and a van. I'd talk to the clients and check the work. Lena says I'd be a robot foreman, and she's probably right.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but doable if you move now, and tell the lads to learn the robot side while it's coming in.
S3.think: The window for my own firm is about three years, enough to make money and buy kit but not to retire on. After that, the firm might be a few robots and me.
S3.do: Asks Pete about buying into his firm, using savings and a small loan to be repaid in three years. Puts money into robot tools as soon as they're good and learns to run and price robot jobs.
S3.feel: Uneasy but up for it, like a big job with a tight deadline.
S3.quote: Lena says I'd be a robot foreman, and she's probably right.
S3.fieldNote: Five years revives his business plan in a new form: buying into his boss's firm and running it with robots. He's cautious about debt and sets a three-year limit. He sees himself as client contact and checker rather than builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to adjust if you're sensible. I'd tell people not to panic and not to ignore it either. I'd say the same to Pete, that it's time to plan the handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is great for me. I'd have my own firm for a good five or six years before robots can do it all, and I'd be ready to use them when they come. I'd be 37 and hopefully have something to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go solo or buy into Pete's firm within the year, and do a short business course at the college so I'm not winging the accounts. I'd buy kit step by step, scanner first, then robot tools as they prove themselves. I'd keep three months in the bank at all times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hopefully have something to sell. Sell to whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bigger firm, or someone who wants a local name with good reviews. Even if robots do the building, people want a firm they trust. That's the bit I'd build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being up in the loft with the radio on, working out how some idiot in 1970 managed to cut through a joist. That's the fun bit. I'd still want to go up there now and then.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to adjust if you're sensible, and tell people not to panic or ignore it. I'd tell Pete it's time to plan the handover.
S4.think: Ten years is great for me, giving five or six years of my own firm before robots can do it all. I'd be 37 and hopefully have something to sell.
S4.do: Goes solo or buys into Pete's firm within the year, and takes a short business course at the college. Buys kit step by step and keeps three months of bills in the bank.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a long runway.
S4.quote: Even if robots do the building, people want a firm they trust.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline fits his business plan almost perfectly. He thinks the lasting value is reputation, not the work itself. He still wants the hands-on puzzle of old houses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan disappears and I'd be stuck with three months' savings and no edge. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small firms to buy the new kit, so it's not only big companies that get the robots. And some income support while people sort themselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the customers. If AGI hits everyone, who's paying for a loft conversion? I've been thinking about the tools, but the clients matter just as much.

headlineQuote: I love the puzzle of an old house, every one's been botched by someone different over 80 years.
portrait: David Garcia is a 27-year-old renovation carpenter at a small loft conversion firm who uses AI every day for pricing, ordering and client emails. He lives with Lena, a primary teacher, has about three months saved and plans to run his own firm by about 30. He's calm when AI fizzles or changes things steadily, seeing steady change as his chance to compete with big builders. AGI in two years makes him anxious because his edge disappears, so he'd stay employed and save. With five or ten years he'd buy into his boss's firm and run it with robots, building a name clients trust.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his business plan would disappear and he'd be left with three months' savings and no edge.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants so small firms can buy the new kit, and some income support while people sort themselves out.
